message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Business Case: Self-Checkout Expansion
Northfield Grocers, prepared for the Executive Committee, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper asks the Executive Committee to approve capital of £1.34 million to install self-checkout lanes in the 14 Northfield stores that do not yet have them, bringing all 18 stores onto the same front-end format by the end of Q3 2026. The recommendation rests on a ten-month pilot in four stores, which began in May 2025.

2. Background
Front-end labour is our second-largest controllable cost after stock. Staffed checkout hours have risen 9% over two years while transaction counts have been flat, largely because of minimum-wage increases and the difficulty of rostering part-time staff for evening peaks. Queue length is also the most frequent complaint in our customer feedback system, cited in 31% of negative comments in 2025.

The four pilot stores (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley) were chosen because they had been fully refurbished in early 2025 and had the floor space to accommodate a six-kiosk bank without removing shelving. Each received six kiosks and retained two staffed lanes.

3. Pilot results
Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:

Metric | Pilot stores | Other stores
Staffed checkout hours per week (change) | -95 hours per store | +3 hours per store
Average queue time at peak | 2.1 min (from 4.6) | 4.4 min (from 4.5)
Shrink as % of sales | 1.2% (from 1.2%) | 1.3% (from 1.3%)
Average basket value (change) | +6% | +2%
Customer satisfaction, front end (index) | 78 (from 71) | 72 (from 72)

The reduction in staffed hours was achieved without redundancies, through natural turnover and redeployment of colleagues into online order picking. Shrink did not move, which addresses the main concern raised when the pilot was approved. Front-end satisfaction rose seven points in the pilot stores and was flat elsewhere.

The rise in average basket value is the most encouraging result. Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit. We have not built this revenue effect into the financial case below, but it represents meaningful upside.

4. Costs
Kiosks cost £14,500 each including the scanning scale and payment terminal. At six kiosks per store, the hardware cost is £87,000 per store, or £1,218,000 for 14 stores. Installation, electrical work and fit-out are quoted at £9,000 per store, a further £126,000, giving total capital of £1,344,000.

Ongoing maintenance and software licensing are quoted at £4,800 per store per year, or £67,200 across the 14 stores.

5. Savings
We assume each new store achieves the same 95-hour weekly reduction as the pilot stores, which is about 12% of a typical store's front-end hours. At a fully loaded front-end cost of £15.20 per hour, this is £1,444 per store per week, or £75,088 per store per year. Across 14 stores, gross labour savings are £1,051,232 per year.

After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432. Against capital of £1,344,000, the investment pays back in about 14 months, well inside the group's 24-month hurdle for store equipment.

6. Risks
Supply. The vendor has confirmed lead times of eight weeks, consistent with completion in Q3.

Customer acceptance. Older customers in some rural stores may prefer staffed lanes. Every store will keep at least two staffed lanes, and a colleague will be assigned to the kiosk bank at peak times, as in the pilot.

Labour transition. As in the pilot, reductions will be achieved through turnover and redeployment rather than redundancy. Annual front-end staff turnover across the estate is 38%, well above the 12% reduction in hours required, so we do not expect to need a consultation process.

7. Recommendation
The pilot has shown that self-checkout cuts peak queue times by more than half, holds shrink flat, improves customer satisfaction and lifts basket value, while delivering labour savings that repay the investment in little over a year. We recommend that the Committee approve capital of £1.34 million and a rollout to all 14 remaining stores, sequenced by store size, to complete by the end of September 2026.
</document>
response:
# Review: Self-Checkout Expansion Business Case

## Errors to fix before this goes to the Committee

**1. The net savings figure is wrong, and it flatters the case (Section 5).**
Gross savings are £1,051,232 and maintenance is £67,200. The paper adds them (£1,118,432) instead of subtracting.
- Correct net savings: £1,051,232 − £67,200 = **£984,032 per year**.
- Correct payback: £1,344,000 ÷ £984,032 ≈ 1.37 years, or **about 16.4 months**, not 14.
- It still clears the 24-month hurdle, but "in little over a year" in Section 7 should become "in about 16 months".

**2. The pilot store count is inconsistent (Section 3).**
The text says "Across the three pilot stores", but Section 2 and the Purpose say four, and it names four (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme, Wexley). Either the wording is a typo or one store's data is missing from the results. Please confirm which.

## Weaknesses in the argument

**3. The basket value claim is overstated.**
The paper says faster checkout "shows" customers buy more. The data show only that basket value rose faster in the pilot stores. The pilot stores were also the ones refurbished in early 2025, so the refurbishment, store selection and local demand are all plausible causes. The same confound applies to the satisfaction gain. I'd soften this to "is consistent with" or add a control. It's reasonable that the upside is excluded from the financials.

**4. The pilot stores may not represent the other 14.**
They were chosen because they were freshly refurbished and had floor space for six kiosks without removing shelving. The paper assumes the other 14 stores can take the same layout and deliver the same 95-hour reduction. If some need shelving removed or layout changes, the £9,000 per store installation estimate and the savings both look optimistic. A store-by-store feasibility check is needed.

**5. Redeployment may not be a real saving.**
Section 3 says the hours reduction came partly through redeploying colleagues into online picking. If those staff are still paid, the cost moves rather than disappears. It counts as a saving only if it avoids hiring that would otherwise have happened. The paper should show how much of the 95 hours is true cost reduction versus reallocation. Related to this, Section 6 relies on 38% turnover to avoid redundancies, but turnover will be uneven across stores and roles, so some stores may not be able to absorb a 12% cut.

**6. The financial case is incomplete.**
- There is no kiosk useful life, depreciation or replacement assumption.
- Training, rollout disruption, and extra costs for the kiosk-bank colleague at peak aren't mentioned.
- There is no sensitivity analysis. For example, how long is payback if only 60–70% of the hours saving is achieved? It would still likely meet the hurdle, which would strengthen the case.

**7. Shrink needs more care.**
Flat shrink over ten months in four stores is encouraging, but it's a small sample, and shrink at self-checkout is often slow to emerge. Say whether it is monitored post-rollout and what the trigger would be for action.

## Minor points

- **Section 2:** Minimum-wage increases raise the cost per hour, not the number of hours. The sentence on rising hours needs a different explanation, or should say cost instead.
- **Section 6 (supply):** Eight-week lead time says nothing about installation capacity. Fitting out 14 stores in the window is a separate constraint from vendor lead time, so the plan should cover installer capacity and sequencing.
- **Timeline:** The paper is dated March 2026 and targets completion by end of September 2026. If it is being considered now, that schedule has passed and needs re-baselining.
- **Section 3:** The "Other stores" column implies a comparison group, but it doesn't say whether it covers all 14 non-pilot stores or a subset.

## What checks out

The capital arithmetic is correct: £87,000 and £1,218,000 hardware, £126,000 installation, £1,344,000 total, and £67,200 maintenance. So are 95 hours × £15.20 = £1,444 per week and £75,088 per year per store, and £1,051,232 across 14 stores. The queue reduction (4.6 to 2.1 min, 54%), the seven-point satisfaction gain, and the 3× basket growth ratio all hold.

**Overall:** the conclusion probably survives the payback correction, since 16 months is still under the 24-month hurdle. But the paper needs the arithmetic fixed, the store-count inconsistency resolved, and the causal and transferability claims toned down or supported.
